data.title: Libice – the main hillfort of the Slavník dynasty (Czech Republic)
data.excerpt: Libice, the main hillfort of the Slavníks – one of the most powerful dynasties in early medieval Bohemia – was the centre of a large territory in eastern Bohemia, set on a rise near the confluence of the Elbe and the Cidlina. It was not only a princely seat and an administrative centre but also a place where Slavník denarii were struck, and in 995 the Přemyslids destroyed it and killed its defenders in one of the oldest massacres in Czech history.

children.text: Libice, the main hillfort of the Slavníks, one of the most powerful dynasties in Bohemia in the Early Middle Ages, was the centre of a larger territory that the Slavníks controlled in eastern Bohemia. It lay on a rise not far from the confluence of the Elbe and the Cidlina. Libice, however, was not only the seat of a princely dynasty and the administrative centre of a principality, but also a place where Slavník denarii were struck.

The area of the bailey of the later Slavník hillfort was already occupied in the Late Bronze Age. Archaeological finds have proved the presence of people of the Tumulus, Lusatian and Knovíz cultures, but finds from the Roman period also come from the eastern tip of the bailey. After a short transitional period, a Slavic population settled at Libice in the 6th century and brought with it pottery of the Prague type. In the course of the 8th century the population demonstrably grew, and in the 9th century a well-fortified hillfort already stood here. Two phases of the defences were identified. The earlier fortification consisted of an earthen rampart with a grillage and an outer stone wall. In the second phase a rampart with three rows of chambers 4.5 m wide was built, and both the inner and the outer defensive wall were constructed of marlstone (opuka). A wide ditch ran in front of the rampart. The first specific mention of the Slavníks comes in the Chronicle of Cosmas, under the year 981, when Prince Slavník is said to have died. Throughout the Slavník period the bailey was densely occupied, and a church of the Virgin Mary with a small cemetery around it also stood here. Later it was given a Gothic form and in 1774–1777 it was rebuilt in the High Baroque style. In connection with the Josephine reforms, however, it was abolished, and today it serves as a parish house. In the south-eastern part of the bailey another building was uncovered, probably a priest’s house, and on the site of today’s cemetery church of St Adalbert a church dedicated to St Boniface probably already stood in the 10th century.

Inside the defences of the acropolis itself, the investigation documented greater building activity in the middle of the 10th century. Specifically, the foundation masonry of a church of the second half of the 10th century was uncovered. It was a single-nave building of Ottonian type with a transept with two galleries and a short chancel ending in an apse. In the space between this apse and the southern arm of the transept, the masonry of two small rooms was found, apparently a baptistery and a sacristy. In the immediate vicinity of the church on its southern side, the remains of a timber building were identified, considered to be the Slavník palace, which was connected to the church. The complete destruction of the hillfort in 995, which is supported by written sources, was also demonstrated. A castellan’s house was then newly built on the site of the Slavník palace. The hillfort was restored as well, though this time as a Přemyslid strongpoint whose defences were not as massive as the previous ones. The castellan was active here until around 1120, when he transferred his seat to the bailey. In the course of the 12th century the declining Libice hillfort lost both its function and its importance and disappeared from the written sources. Only in 1228 is Libice mentioned as a village in the possession of the Convent of St George at Prague Castle.

children.text: Libice has been at the centre of scholarly attention since the 16th century. Specialist investigations were carried out at the end of the 19th century by Josef Ladislav Píč and later by Jan Hellich. In 1949–1953 a detailed archaeological investigation of the site was carried out by Dr Rudolf Turek of the National Museum, during which not only the remains of buildings but also many very valuable objects were uncovered, which attest to the very high cultural level of the inhabitants of the Slavník hillfort. Small objects that survived even the violent destruction of the site document Libice’s lively trade contacts not only with the whole of Bohemia but also with Great Moravia, and imports from the Viking, Carolingian and Balkan spheres even came to light. The finds portray the Libice of the second half of the 10th century as a flourishing, prosperous hillfort, a centre of trade, culture and church life.

In 1961 the Libice hillfort was declared an archaeological monument reserve, in 1979 a protective zone was established, and the acropolis of the hillfort itself has been protected as a national cultural monument since 1989. Since 1974 the Institute of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences has carried out annual rescue archaeological excavations in the bailey, and to date just under 6% of the area of the bailey has been investigated in this way. These excavations map in detail the development of the fortification during the 10th century. An aerial survey of the site carried out in 2000 brought a series of insights into the internal layout of the acropolis and provided impulses for further research. Several cemeteries were recorded in the area of the hillfort and its surroundings, in which burial took place throughout the Early Middle Ages. Burials of members of the higher social strata, who demonstrably already inclined towards Christianity, were frequently identified. The most important event of recent times in the area of the acropolis was the placing of a bronze statuary group of St Adalbert and St Gaudentius in the immediate vicinity of the uncovered masonry of the church in 2000. The placing of the group was preceded by a rescue archaeological excavation.

From the point of view of heritage protection, the primary task at this site is to secure the archaeological find spot in the area of the acropolis and to prevent undesirable interventions in the underlying terrain layers of the bailey (the village of Libice).

children.text: Who were the Slavníks? It is presumably above all those born later, who no longer had a joint Czech–Slovak history class at school, who do not know the Slavník dynasty and its tragic fate during the consolidation of the early feudal Czech state at all. I shall therefore permit myself a brief excursion into this slightly obscure period in the history of the Přemyslids and take a closer look at one of the greatest and oldest massacres in Czech history, which ultimately contributed to the consolidation of the power of the Přemyslid dynasty.

children.text: First it is necessary to shed light on the situation in the Bohemia of the princes at that time. After the death of St Wenceslas, his brother Boleslav I took power. This began the era of the principality’s rise. Boleslav managed to free himself from subjection to the Frankish Empire and became its partner (his „help“ at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955). The Czech state became a significant power of central Europe after it succeeded in occupying Silesia and the Kraków region and in penetrating as far as the present-day borders of Belarus. In these areas the prince had the inhabitants „caught“, and they were later sold as slaves in Prague. In addition, a long-distance merchant route ran through there, and by controlling it the Přemyslids also gained profits. Most of the money from the sales went to the princely army, whose commanders were scattered across the whole territory of the principality. As later turned out, the system was not very stable.

The rise of the Slavník dynasty began in the second half of the 10th century. Before the massacre they held an area in eastern Bohemia. Their centre was the hillfort of Libice nad Cidlinou. A marriage, otherwise unknown in detail, confirms their ties to the Saxon imperial dynasty. It can be assumed that the Saxon dynasty wanted to have in the Slavníks a Czech counterweight to the Přemyslids, and it must be said that the Slavníks were certainly not against it. They managed to install Adalbert – a member of the Slavník dynasty – in the office of Bishop of Prague. By then the times were already changing. The prince was Boleslav’s son of the same name — Boleslav II. Under him the bishopric of Prague was founded, and its first bishop was a Saxon familiar with Slovak conditions — Thietmar. The second bishop, for diplomatic reasons, was the Slavník Adalbert. Making enemies of the Slavníks could have cost the Přemyslids dearly.

The violent act took place in 995. At that time Adalbert had already been away from Bohemia for a year after disagreements with the prince. Tension between the ruling Přemyslids and the ambitious Slavníks was growing. This „competition“ was not the only reason.

A crisis was beginning to show in Bohemia. The principality began to lose the possessions it had gained a generation earlier. It lost Lesser Poland, Kraków and, around the year 990 (Polish scholars assume the preceding decades), Silesia. Princely revenues thus fell, and the soldiers then did (not) receive them. The soldiers who managed to escape from Silesia did not improve the situation either. A weak economy based on subjugated territories could not feed the princely army. Morale was bad as well. A drastic act could improve the damaged morale of the retinue and bring money from Slavník territory. A further reason was the power ambitions of yet another family, this time the Vršovci.

The sixty-year-old, gravely ill ruler issued the order to destroy the Slavníks, also because of the strong pressure of the other magnates (and allegedly also in connection with his fits of rage and derangement). In any case, he exploited the situation perfectly.

The German emperor was preparing a campaign against the pagan Obotrites. The Czechs sent two contingents. One was sent by the Přemyslids and was led by the prince’s son — Boleslav the Red (later Prince Boleslav III). The other (the Slavník one) was led by Slavník’s eldest son, Soběbor. The seat of the Slavníks — Libice — was left without experienced warriors, with only a small garrison. It was commanded by four brothers. They were: Spytimír, Dobraslav, Porej and Čáslav.

On 27 September 995 the attack on Libice began under the leadership of the Vršovci. The retinue scattered the people of the surrounding area and besieged Libice. The defenders did not want to fight on the day before the feast of St Wenceslas, but the attackers did not allow them that. A fierce fight began, in which, despite their courage, the defenders stood no chance. They had to take refuge in the church. The attackers gave them hope that they would be left alive. As soon as they came out of the church, they were all killed, including the women and children.

The only two Slavníks who survived — Adalbert and Soběbor — lived out their lives in Poland in the asylum of Bolesław the Brave. Libice was granted to the Vršovci, but in 1108 the same fate befell them. They too were massacred. The death of Boleslav II (999) began a crisis in the principality, during which the ruler changed several times. Moravia was conquered by the Polish ruler Bolesław the Brave (who for a while also became prince of Bohemia), and he held it until 1019.
